speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There is also greater focus and awareness of the move towards not just fair, but progressive workplaces and employment practices by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) and our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, anecdotally, when I meet fellow PMEs, I am still hearing complaints of two kinds.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the hiring-of-own-kind practices and companies advertising in the Jobs Bank for the sake of advertising and treating FCF and the Jobs Bank as mere window dressing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This happens not just in big multinational companies (MNCs), but also small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some also share with me that employment agencies and placement companies are also where some of these malpractices happen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The general concern is over the glaring disproportionate number of foreign PMEs in certain sectors and companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In some cases, the nationality bias results in job losses of local PMEs and hiring of foreign PMEs for jobs which local PMEs can fill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also know he has been having coffee with some of these employers and businesses on the "watch list".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Has there been an improvement since the last time he shared about this "watch list" and can he share who these companies are?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As I am also very concerned with the placement rate from the Jobs Banks, I have three concrete suggestions for MOM, in respect of what we can do to tackle those companies with the "double weaks", to better strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Suggestion one – to put a clamp on companies with discriminatory practices, I propose a company-specific and tiered approach which can be scaled up to the industry level, if needed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Level 1 involves stringent scrutiny of companies which display the two "weaks".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Those with a weak Singaporean Core and a weak commitment to hire and develop Singaporeans will be identified and differentiated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Stricter Employment Pass (EP) application conditions and requirements are to be enforced on these companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Page: 74 Level 2 involves suspending all EP applications of the companies identified at Level 1 which continue to show a disregard or weak commitment to hire and develop a Singaporean Core and turn a deaf ear to warnings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Level 3 involves imposing a PME dependency ratio.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Should companies remain recalcitrant, a company-specific PME dependency ratio can be put in place as a final option.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Suggestion two – to encourage building a strong Singaporean Core, companies which outsource some of their services, such as information technology (IT), human resource (HR) or accounting and even construction projects, can, within the terms of the tender or contract prescribe that there must be a Singaporean Core in the workforce of that entity bidding for the contract or tender.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest the public sector can take the lead in this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Suggestion three – over and above existing requirements under the law, there could be tighter regulation and accreditation of employment and placement agencies to weed out biased and unfair hiring-of-own-kind practices and ensuring a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, these agencies, recruitment companies and even company HR departments should not and must not treat the advertising requirement as mere window dressing and their practices should be closely monitored.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Their frontline and placement staff should undergo mandatory training and accreditation to understand the concept of building the Singaporean Core and the objectives of both FCF and the Jobs Bank.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the converse, I suggest that MOM also recognise and offer carrots to those companies and businesses which demonstrate an exemplary and progressive Singaporean Core and a resolute commitment to hire and develop Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   I have three suggestions regarding how to strengthen the Singaporean Core of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, for individual companies, I propose a company-specific approach to eliminate the discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Level 1 involves those companies that have the double "weaks".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Stricter criteria are to be applied when they apply for EPs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At Level 2, if those companies identified at Level 1 turn a deaf ear to warnings, we will suspend the application of their EPs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At Level 3, should the companies remain recalcitrant, a PME dependency ratio can be imposed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, prescribe in the outsourced contract certain rules and regulations to make sure that contractors build a team of staff with Singaporeans as their core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The public sector can take the lead in this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, make sure employment agencies advertise job vacancies according to the legal requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: They are worried for fellow Singaporean workers, especially their family members, neighbours and friends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Our older workers are also worried about the current economic slowdown, as they feel that they are the ones that are going to be affected the most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: There are companies which have the locals' interest in their hearts, although they have a regular EP inflow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are also companies whose hearts are not with our locals, where I received feedback that they use the locals in filling up the numbers and are not particularly interested in developing our local workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Allow me to continue my speech in Malay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, in my interactions with the Malay community in Nee Soon and in events organised by Malay/Muslim bodies, just like other Singaporeans, they expressed concern about an economic slowdown.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: They are worried that their jobs, as well as the jobs of their family members and friends, will be affected by an economic slowdown.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Some businesses have expressed doubt that they could ever expand even if demand for their businesses increases, shortage of workers being the main constraint to growth.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Nonetheless, many SMEs in the services sectors have realised that relying on manpower to grow their businesses is not a long-term solution.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: They are responding to the Government's call to raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Page: 76 SMEs are seeking ways to improve, to become more efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: For most, improvements made are piecemeal and incremental, often not significant enough to eliminate existing headcounts or avoid new hiring.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Not surprisingly, therefore, only SMEs which undertake fundamental changes revamping their business models stand a good chance to succeed and become manpower lean.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Implementation experiences from SMEs attempting major revamps often suggest that manpower loading can become worse before it gets better.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: This is because businesses need to maintain two parallel systems until the new one stabilises and can replace the old system.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: How would the Ministry address SMEs' needs for additional manpower during their transformation efforts?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Apart from helping individual SMEs, does the Ministry see any benefits of grouping SMEs of the same industry for effective intervention?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Businesses have high hopes that ITPs will be able to meet sectoral needs because of their customised nature.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: While recognising that there is much we need to do in embracing technology and modern management as part of the restructuring, some businesses are also worried whether we will have the right quantity and quality of workers and skills to support the restructuring efforts.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Given that our labour participation rate is already almost the highest in the world, our indigenous workforce growth tapering off, businesses question if we should selectively let in foreign talents with skillsets to strengthen our Singapore Core, to render our workforce more competent and versatile overall.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Aligning our HR development strategy and skills upgrading programmes with ITP is, therefore, the best way to ensure success in our economic restructuring.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: The close working relations among the public and private sectors and the unions are pivotal.

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: In this regard, may I ask how the Ministry is involving the tripartite partners in the development of ITP and their roadmaps?

speaker: Mr Lee Yi Shyan (East Coast)
text: Would MOM officers be represented in the Transformation Champions to co-drive ITP?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In a recent Straits Times article, it was reported that higher-skilled workers make up the bulk of layoffs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is quite disturbing as one would have expected that higher-skilled workers would have less difficulty keeping their jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Given that the economic lookout for the next year appears much weaker, I am concerned that more Singaporeans, especially PMETs, will find themselves displaced and unable to find another equally well-paying job.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: What about efforts by the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and the Community Development Councils in helping Singaporeans find employment?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would there be a report card on their efficacy?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Minister also comment on whether companies are simply complying with the rules without making any real efforts to help Singaporeans find jobs?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If so, what can MOM do to discourage such companies which are not sincere in providing employment for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Send a strong signal to these companies that there are serious consequences for flouting the rules.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Minister also share how we can tweak our policies to ensure that Singaporeans are able to find alternative jobs quickly if they are retrenched or lose their jobs due to no fault of theirs?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Government to ensure that Singaporeans should always remain the core of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many other countries have similar retrenchment compensation laws.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I know that this will have a financial impact on the companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The details can be worked out so that the financial burden would not be too heavy on the companies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Good afternoon, Mdm Chair, fellow Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For example, when PMETs from MNCs sought employment with SMEs recently, employers hesitated because of their "high education, high position and high pay".

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: PMETs on the other hand, felt that the environment and benefits of local SMEs are not as good.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They were stranded in a situation of mismatched expectations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On one hand, SMEs are unable to hire talents while, on the other hand, PMETs are unable to find employment.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To allow everyone in the workforce to have a role to play, the Government, businesses and individuals need to seriously seek out the reasons and come up with countermeasures.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: An SME business owner once told me that he would very much like to transform.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: He has attended courses and even hired consultants, but he ultimately needs an assistant to help in the Page: 78 execution.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Taking advantage of the current environment, when SMEs are able to recruit experienced PMETs on board, the boss would have found a capable assistant.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Please allow me to use the famous Chinese classic novel "Romance of the Three Kingdoms" as an analogy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Liu Bei was also an "SME" and only managed to recruit Zhuge Liang after three attempts.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: From then, his "business" developed rapidly and even managed to contend with the "larger corporation" headed by Cao Cao.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As the situation of an ageing population escalates, businesses will face a more severe manpower challenge.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I belong to the post-war Baby Boom generation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The total population of this category of more than 900,000 – making up around a quarter of the population – is now moving on to the retirement phase.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: When this generation of people was younger, it happened to be the time when our country started attracting many MNCs and embarked on rapid economic development.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs can take this opportunity to attract more well-educated talents into their companies.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs used to provide supporting services to MNCs but through transformation, they can now grow to become promising Singapore enterprises which can provide a more stable career path to its employees than MNCs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, SMEs need to create higher-quality job opportunities in order to attract these talents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs felt disappointed with the publicity on skills upgrading in these two years.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the news reports on encouraging skills upgrading that I often read consist of Institute of Technical Education (ITE) students being placed in important roles by MNCs after working hard to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: During the recruitment process, SME owners not only cannot afford to hire graduates, they find it difficult to attract tertiary students and face restrictions on employing foreign talents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Now that even the ITE students are all going to MNCs, who else can they hire?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To my knowledge, many polytechnic and ITE graduates have been entrusted with important roles, assuming major responsibilities in SMEs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We should not give SMEs the perception that only MNCs provide career opportunities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Another publicity that requires adjustment is skills upgrading vis-à-vis pay increments.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Upgrading of skills is to correspond with the upgrading of enterprise and the needs of the industry, which, in turn, increases employability.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, this does not naturally equate to pay increments.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some jobs have become obsolete or redundant, thus, employees need to acquire new skills in order to remain employable.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If yes, I hope the Government can develop training content according to the actual needs of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I would also like to urge the TACs from the various industries to participate in the SMPs proactively to develop more talents for the practical needs of local SMEs through the Government Page: 79 (public), enterprises (private) and TACs model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: MOM spearheads the complex and demanding role of realising these goals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, its officers have ramped up the activity on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry's efforts over the last few years have bought us valuable lead time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the situation on the ground becomes increasingly complex, I would like to ask about its use of analytics to expand its capacity to monitor the labour market situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: On the one hand, it is clear that some companies are experiencing problems with the restrictions on supply of foreign manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, there are also reports of over-representation of foreign manpower in certain instances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although the overall evidence suggests that such problems are not widespread, why are these two extremes occurring at the same time?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Are they symptomatic of some deeper flaw in our system?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is our labour market infrastructure up to the task of incorporating the participation of foreign manpower for the longer term?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is it possible to use data from the Jobs Bank as well as other labour market transactions to examine these problems, to understand if they are problems of matching?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, could the Ministry assemble data on hiring experiences to properly understand if there are differences between the jobs matching process for locals and foreigners?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, analytics plays a crucial role, because it is possible to build into such an analysis complete anonymity while preserving the broad patterns that are of interest in voluminous transactions data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The reason why I am raising this is because the pendulum seems to have swung in the other direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The chorus of voices against foreign manpower is growing louder by the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Are we sure we are moving in the right direction?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Are we sure we are not swinging too far in the opposite direction?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I welcome initiatives like the Career Support Programme (CSP).

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It benefits both employer and employee with wage subsidy as well as it allows employers time to assess the competency of the employee while it provides the employee the appropriate support for training and skills upgrading in that one year.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the current changes and the impact of technology, the workforce may not be able to keep up, reskill or upskill fast enough.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With this, we must recognise that there will be skills gaps.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while we need companies to build the Singapore Core, we must recognise that businesses do need time to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For companies that are committed with a clear plan and commitment to invest in building a Singapore Core, can MOM take a differentiated approach and provide greater support to these organisations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As restructuring and reskilling require time and resources, can MOM allow for transitional manpower adjustments during that period?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will allow the time and access to resources to train and to advance the skills transfer to the local workforce to build a strong Singapore Core.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Minster Lim Swee Say had described the ideal situation as when local and foreign PMEs do not compete with each other for jobs in Singapore but rather work together to compete for jobs with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this moment, there are still frequent complaints about foreigners doing jobs here that can be performed by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Ministry share how serious the situation is?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is being done to ensure that EPs complement rather than compete with locals, and what more can we do?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are we going to have stricter EP application conditions and requirements to manage the EP inflow?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Ministry look into how long a particular job has been filled by a foreigner?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In cases where it is necessary to hire foreigners, we should ensure that foreign companies execute transfers of skills and expertise to Singaporean employees over time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If a foreigner is replaced by yet another foreigner after a number of years, I would suggest the company be interviewed so that MOM can find out why the transfer of duties to a Singaporean had failed to take place and what can be done to rectify this.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry share with us the success and challenges of the various schemes for retrenched PMETs and the National Jobs Bank?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How successful is PCP in helping retrenched PMETs find jobs in growth sectors and is there scope to increase the number of PCPs?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The culture of an organisation, including its hiring practices, is set by the owner or chief executive.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Ministry's senior management should consider having more frequent dialogues and meetings with the owner or chief executive to talk about their hiring practices, starting from the "double weak" and "weak" companies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will enhance mutual understanding of the employment situation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For PMEs who are referred to career counselling programme, we should ensure that the counsellors are more senior and possess more experience than the PMEs that come for this programme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They could also take on the role of a mentor, in addition to counselling and career guidance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The counsellors could be senior management or senior officers of the Ministry, industry TACs or volunteers who possess management experience.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This could also be a hiring opportunity Page: 81 for these counsellors if they find the PMEs a good match to their organisation's needs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would also like to ask whether more could be done for non-PMETs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They would need career counselling and time to adjust to new training to help them handle new jobs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Interim financial assistance should be paired with job advisory and placement to help them tide over the difficult time between jobs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I had previously asked the Minister to consider a "carrot" approach to recognise and reward companies that have demonstrated and continue to develop a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My point is that beyond the cash incentives and support, it is possible to have a nuanced recognition and reward system.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the tight labour market, while there are still job opportunities, the biggest challenge for PMETs has been gaps in skill or experience to match the available jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: A higher proportion of PMETs are finding it difficult to secure employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Employers are facing challenges finding the right resources to hire for jobs that they need to fill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Apart from efforts of SkillsFuture to help workers gain experience and skills required for available job opportunities, what more can be done to achieve more effective matching of the required skills upgrading and Singaporeans to jobs, especially for mature PMETs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Many employers, especially SMEs, have expressed that they are facing challenges attracting suitable Singaporeans to fill the jobs they are hiring for.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can more be done in this area for job matching programmes for SMEs to tap on to get the right skills and support for job matching?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How will the job matching and placements be done and how can Singaporeans interested in the job opportunities in the ICT sector be able to tap on the programme?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it is understood that not all of these positions can be filled by Singaporeans, I find it too convenient to ask Singaporeans to accept that Page: 82 we would need foreigners to fill these positions because we do not have enough babies born annually or there are just not enough Singaporeans who join the workforce each year.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are more than enough Singaporeans who are retrenched from their jobs in industries that have been negatively impacted by the slowing domestic market and global economy, or those who have been displaced because of increased mechanisation, "technologisation" and "informatisation" of industries, for instance, those in the marine and process or manufacturing sectors and even those in administrative or management positions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of them are in their 40s or 50s, while some are in their 60s but who are still keen to be employed.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once retrenched and displaced, they settle for unskilled or lower-skilled jobs, such as cleaning tables or the streets or taking food orders, and accepting salaries which are a fraction of what they used to earn.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also propose that our PCP be extended to help reskill and upskill Singaporeans to join or return to the engineering profession.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a recent job fair in Ang Mo Kio Group Representation Constituency, I was talking to the HR manager of a local company that specialises in roadworks and construction.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Well-paying jobs are there for Singaporeans but there may be a substantial mismatch of skills and experience in order to qualify for such jobs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: PCP can help to plug this gap and bring back some engineers who have switched careers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet another group of Singaporeans that serves as a valuable manpower resource is our retirees and stay-at-home mothers (SAHMs).

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the current shortage of childcare educarers and caregivers for the elderly, I am sure we can develop and pilot a training programme for our retirees and SAHMs to be trained as babysitters, child minders, educarers or caregivers for the elderly.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should seriously explore this and find effective ways in bringing back to the workforce our retirees Page: 83 and SAHMs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we better support workers in transition across jobs and industries?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to ask if MOM could provide some form of wage support beyond the training allowance for working people in transition under the Job Placement and Training Programmes to encourage more to move to growth areas in the various industries.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: More coordination between the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and the industry to ensure maximum linkage between Pre-Employment Training and Continuing Education and Training is important.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Increasingly, it would be a challenge for fresh school leavers to secure a job upon their graduation unless enterprises provide opportunities to these school leavers under the SkillsFuture Earn and Learn Programme.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Companies need to change their mental models of seeking experienced workers even though applicants may have the right attitude and passion for the job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I shall now speak about the National Jobs Bank.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It would be good to know the success rates of Singaporeans who managed to find a job through the National Jobs Bank.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry monitor the impact that the National Jobs Bank has brought about in supporting the Singaporean Core objective?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Just like Mr Chong Kee Hiong, if the intent is to ensure Singaporeans are considered and hired for well-paying good jobs, the question arises if it is necessary to exempt jobs that pay more than $12,000 in the portal and if this serves the intended purpose.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, there needs to be further review to examine the impact of the National Jobs Bank and if it requires further enhancement, such as the 14-day duration of job posting and classification of jobs based on sectors, so that it serves the well-intended purpose of supporting FCF.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I shall now talk about uplifting the professionalism of HR practitioners in SMEs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With evolving economic needs, the HR professionals' role is also evolving to be a demanding one.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: HR practitioners must, therefore, be on top of their profession to play an effective role, especially those employed in SMEs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can I ask the Minister if there can be specific mandatory training programmes designed for these HR professionals to update them on current laws and best practices?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is also timely as we will soon be introducing the Employment Claims Tribunal (ECT) to settle disputes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Following the passing of the Protection from Harassment Bill in Parliament in 2014 to better protect people from harassment and anti-social behaviour, a Tripartite Workgroup on Prevention of Harassment at the Workplace was set up to ensure workplaces are safe for all employees.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Coming from the healthcare sector, this issue is close to my heart.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many frontline healthcare workers often have to face the brunt of distressed patients and their families, yet are afraid and reluctant to speak Page: 84 up for fear of retaliation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: An organisation cannot function effectively when workers are afraid.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Following the release of the Tripartite Advisory to encourage employers to put in place procedures to manage workplace harassment and develop a harassment prevention policy as part of their risk management process, can more be done to encourage sectors in high risk, for example, public services, to take the lead in fostering a conducive and safe organisational culture?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We have extended many efforts in promoting workplace safety and enforcing compliance, especially in the recent year.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are employers who are still taking a complacent stand and, as a result, putting the lives of many innocent workers at risk, which also affects their families.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What new measures are taken to address the concerns of workplace safety proactively?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It has to be a collective concerted effort of all parties in the society.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do more to change mindsets, and there is a huge difference between the words "save" and "safe", although both sound almost the same.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some errant employers "save cost" and not provide "safe" workplaces for their workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to identify these irresponsible employers so that potential applicants know who the errant employers are if continuous education and awareness efforts fail to change behaviour and responses.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On hindsight, the Minister can also consider a review of the work-life grant criteria in the interim so that the assistance made available is attractive enough for employers to support flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The sectoral tripartite committee should explore FWAs as an option to attract and retain within their respective industry sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This could be done by sharing best practices and for progressive companies to assist other companies in this regard.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A more concerted effort is needed to make this part of an organisational norm to encourage working people, especially working mothers, to continue to be in the workforce without disruption.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On mandating eldercare or family care leave, we have evolved over the years as a nation to place greater importance on caring for the family, community and society as a whole.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As a cohesive nation, we acknowledge that for this to materialise, there needs to be holistic support for families to grow and the elderly to be cared for by their loved ones.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On supporting mature workers, the last item, during an economic downturn, mature workers in their late 50s most fear losing their jobs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These job losses may be due to cyclical effect or are structural in nature.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is notable that implementation can be a challenge.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With a sectoral approach of reviewing foreign worker quota for each company, perhaps the Ministry can explore this further, if possible.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These scenarios have given rise to several concerns amongst the working population.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am highlighting three areas of concern and offering three suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The first is the rise in the number of PMEs who are facing workplace disputes and issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am aware MOM has started public consultation on the proposed ECT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can there also be a one-stop facility similar to our U PME Centre, or can we use our existing U PME Centre as a front-facing one-stop facility for all PMEs when they require workplace advice or consultation on workplace issues?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, recently, I had an encounter with a unionised company which is in trouble and had been trying to obtain a scheme of arrangement but failed and now applying to Court for judicial management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: It is provided in law that a moratorium is imposed when a company files for insolvency proceedings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This means no proceedings can be taken against that company, unless with the leave of Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: My concern and frustration are with the plight of the workers there.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: What is horrifying is that the workers have been left unpaid their monthly wages since late last year when the insolvency proceedings started.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: They are hanging on to the company hoping that some form of retrenchment benefit can be paid to them or that there are monies to be obtained when the company winds up after a proof of debt is filed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In reality, there are many other secured creditors and the workers may well be unlikely to obtain any retrenchment benefit as the union is unable to take the company to the Industrial Arbitration Court to obtain an order for retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There may also not be any monies left for distribution via section 328 of the Companies Act after the company winds up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In any case, the maximum amount they can get is $12,500 under section 328.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: They will also get nothing if they leave their jobs now.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Many have been with the company for years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am told their Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions are also unpaid for this year and partially for those months late last year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The union has also engaged legal counsel but there is still nothing which can be done.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Is there Page: 86 really nothing which the authorities can do against the company or help the workers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There are about 100 workers still there and many have already left.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In many ways, this is a case where the law provides no recourse for these aggrieved workers who may work for months for free and not paid.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am not sure how long this case will drag on and the end is definitely not soon.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Besides some of the financial assistance schemes by unions and the community, can there be specific legislative provisions or regulations in place or exceptions made to help these workers who are left in the lurch?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By the same token, I know of another company which is planning to wind up later this year and has started to prepare for it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Yet, when asked to negotiate for an agreement on retrenchment payouts, it is simply dragging its feet and waiting for the time to come so that they need not pay a single cent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can the laws be amended such that for disputes on wages and retrenchment benefits, the case can be allowed to proceed for an Industrial Arbitration Court hearing during the period of "moratorium" so as to obtain a judgment or order before the company actually folds.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The third area, unlike traditional contract of service where there is an employer-employee relationship and labour legislation providing protection, there are currently no laws or regulations to help the growing group of freelance professionals in Singapore who are in a contract for service situation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Even the Trade Unions Act prohibit NTUC and our unions to represent them or formally organise them except through the formation of associations which are not unions per se and not vested with powers provided in the Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Not a small group and I expect it to grow with the advent of the sharing economy and the nature of work, workforce, workplaces and work relationships.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have had many engagements with freelance professionals via our PME Unit's events.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The problem we face is that nowhere in the world are there specific laws protecting freelancers and that many freelancers are unable to even band together to form an association.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: They are not allowed to be represented by unions and their only recourse is to the Small Claims Tribunal with a jurisdictional cap.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: NTUC has been trying to assist these freelance professionals and we have started a freelance and self-employed unit and the U-Associate programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat said in his round-up speech that Budget 2016 is but "one step in a long journey".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: From the manpower angle, this is not a walking step but a running step.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Since coming to MOM just about a year ago, I have been asked many questions on our labour policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Employers looking for workers say they cannot find local workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: They ask: can MOM relax on foreign workers, up the quota, down the levy and be more pro-business?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Workers looking for jobs, especially those looking for PMET jobs, say they cannot get the jobs that they want or the promotion they feel they deserve, so they ask: can MOM be more pro-worker?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Why not "Singaporean first", why not "Singaporean Only"?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The profile of jobs has continued to improve.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Local PMET employment now accounts for 54% of our total local employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, these are good employment outcomes for our workers and our people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The next five years will be much more challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are going to see a drop in the growth of the labour force, a sharp and structural drop.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, put together, growth of the Singapore workforce will continue to drop from 4% a year in 2011 to 2014, to 2% last year and likely to be around 1% by the year 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This has a great impact on the future employment landscape in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The days of more than 100,000 job growth a year are over.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: With no gain in productivity, we have moved from a 4+0=4 or 4% growth in the Singapore workforce plus 0% growth in productivity to give us a 4% gross domestic product (GDP) growth during the year 2011 to 2014 on average.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Last year, it dropped to 2+0=2 or 2% workforce growth, 0% growth in productivity to give us a 2% growth in our GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: From 4+0=4 to 2+0=2, what is going to happen next?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Will employment outcomes in the next five years be better or worse?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I can see, I can think of three possible scenarios – the Good, the Bad and, of course, the Ugly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The first scenario, we are unable to transform fast enough; continue with zero productivity growth; continue with manpower-led growth of more than 100,000 jobs a year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: MOM will have no Page: 88 choice, we do a U-turn, relax on our foreign manpower and that is what many employers are asking for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: From 4+0 to 2+0, we now go back to 3+0.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We have to let in more foreign workers to make up for the slower growth in local manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: With 3+0=3, yes, we have 3% GDP growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But what happens to our local to -foreign worker ratio?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: It will continue to drop from the two is to one today, maybe to one is to one, one day and, beyond that, Singaporean workers will become a minority in our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The Singaporean Core will be weakened further and, in fact, the local-foreign divide will deepen further.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: That is why I call it the "Ugly" scenario.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The second scenario, to avoid this ugly outcome, MOM can stand firm, no U-turn in our foreign manpower policy, continue to moderate the intake of foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But without breakthrough in productivity growth, we will move from 4+0 to 2+0 to eventually 1+0=1.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, in other words, low growth will become the new norm, in fact, hovering around stagnation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If that happens, it is a matter of time that unemployment in Singapore will go up and wage growth will stop, and I call this a "Bad" scenario for all.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The third scenario is for us to recognise that technology is changing the nature of jobs and global competition is changing the nature of investment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Instead of manpower-led growth, 100,000 new jobs a year, we go for manpower-lean growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We speed up transformation, instead of going for larger quantity of jobs growth, we go for better quality of job growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Step by step, sector by sector, we move from high value-added to value creation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: From value creation to value multiplication; and then we can return to positive productivity growth again.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Instead of going from 4+0, 2+0 to either 3+0 which is an ugly outcome, or 1+0 which is a bad outcome, we should strive for 1+2, 1% growth in our workforce plus 2% growth in our productivity to give us 3% growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, 1+2=3 is the good outcome that we must strive for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The challenge for us is how to make it happen.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Along the way, if we are more pro-business and less pro-worker, we could end up with a strong economy but a weak Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If we are more pro-worker and less pro-business, we can have a strong Singaporean Core but a weak economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Neither is good because growth cannot be sustained, eventually we will go downhill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: First, to be a more manpower-lean economy and more productive economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is of great concern to MOM because if we fail to become a more manpower-lean economy, manpower will become the bottleneck in our future growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Hence, Industry Transformation Maps are so important for us to visualise the industry of the future, to make better use of technology, manpower, innovation to break the bottlenecks of small size, limited resources, especially manpower limitation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 89 To forge a new mindset of lean transformation, lean innovation, from lean manufacturing to lean services, from lean industry to lean enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mr Lee Yi Shyan and Mr Thomas Chua will be pleased to know that we are giving special attention and support to SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Therefore, we are very determined to speed up LEDS during this slowdown.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: My commitment to SMEs is that those with solid plans, real action to be more manpower-lean and productive, you can be assured of our best support, not just from MOM, but all the other agencies under LEDS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In fact, MOM will also provide transitional flexibility in foreign worker support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This was the point brought up by Mr Lee Yi Shyan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Later, my colleague, Minister of State Teo Ser Luck, will share more on LEDS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Our second thrust is to build a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Every Industry Transformation Map will be accompanied by an SMP formulated by the Sectoral Tripartite Committee.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This will address the concern of Mr Lee Yi Shyan on whether MOM will be involved in co-driving the development of the Industry Transformation Plan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In fact, we will be coordinating our efforts through the SMPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Ms Jessica Tan expressed her concern about whether we can minimise this mismatch between skill and job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: With SMP, we will be able to look ahead and identify what type of jobs will be created, what kind of skills need to be developed for the future, so that we can support the growth of this transformed industry of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In this way, it also helps our people to upgrade, reskill and, along the way, we aim to build a strong Singaporean Core in all major sectors of the economy, as we continue to transform these industries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Those in the hotel industry are fully aware that it is not possible for them to grow the workforce in the hotel sector by 20% because of this keener competition for manpower as we slow down the growth of the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Under the SMP for the hotel sector, we have three priorities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The industries are working very hard to reduce the staff-to-room manning ratio, so that as the room number goes up, you do not have to increase the number of workers at the same proportion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: How to attract, develop, retain and improve the quality of locals working in this sector?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And last but not least, the service transformation into hotels of the future, so that we can remain globally competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In support of this direction by the industry, through the SMP, the NTUC e2i, the Singapore Tourism Board, WDA, unions and the industry associations, we are working very closely together to attract ITE, polytechnic and degree holders under the executive development programme for the hotel sector for them to join the hospitality, F&B and retail sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This was the point brought up Mr Lee Yi Shyan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 90 First, help them to learn supervisory skills, put them through 12 to 18 months of on-the-job training (OJT), so that they can become duty manager, assistant manager and, from there, develop their career.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are also facilitating the mid-career PMETs through professional conversion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: At the same time, we are helping them to become more lean and more productive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For example, rank-and-file workers in the hotel sector are now undergoing this process of multi-skilling, so that each person can perform more than one task, thereby optimising the deployment of manpower and, along the way, help them to enhance their wages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Another example would be through the use of radio frequency identification to strengthen the process of automation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In fact, the Singapore Tourism Board and WDA are now working together with the hotel industry to formulate an initiative to be known as the Lean Hotel Initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In short, make it a movement in our hotel sector, so that the jobs of the future in this hotel sector will become attractive, so that the Singaporean Core will be stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about the ICT sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The ICT sector, under the leadership of the Infocomm Development Authority (IDA), is formulating the SMP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: All the areas of opportunities will be identified and we will step up efforts to channel more Singaporeans into this sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As we speed up industry transformation, redundancy will go up, as seen in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Most are able to find jobs, hence, our low unemployment today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Yet, we are still concerned because we are seeing, among the workers made redundant, there are more mature workers; there are more PMETs, and, in fact, they also need more time to find jobs, especially the mature PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Besides helping to strengthen the Singaporean Core at the sector level, sector by sector, like what we did for the hotel sector, we must also do more to support Singaporean workers at the individual level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We share the concerns of Assoc Prof Muhd Faishal Ibrahim, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Ms Jessica Tan and others, and we will do more to support them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We launched CSP in October last year to encourage employment of mid-career PMETs, especially those who are long-term unemployed, who have been out of a job for more than six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: A mid-career PMET who has been out of job for six months, can come under the CSP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In the last five months, we managed to reach out to 200 mature PMETs who have been out of job for more than six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So far, about half of them have successfully secured employment and most are with SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mr Thomas Chua may be happy to hear this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We have very positive feedback from both employers and employees because, for the employees, they suffer a smaller cut in wages, given the wage support; for the employers, they have to bear lower wage cost, given the subsidies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 91 One example is Mr Kuan Mun Fai, 52 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He was a Business Development Director with an MNC for 23 years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For seven months, he could not find a job that is suitable for him.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He came under the CSP when it was launched in October.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: At that time, he was feeling unsure whether he would be able to get a job that he was looking for.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But today, he is a different person, confident and positive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Under the CSP, within one month, we helped him to find a good job with a local distributor of industrial lighting products to develop markets in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and East Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Yes, he did accept a pay cut to join this company, but he is prepared to work his way up with this new employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For PMETs made redundant and have difficulty finding jobs, meaning six months or more, we will waive the age requirement of 40.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In other words, even the younger PMETs, having been made redundant, if they have difficulty finding jobs for more than six months, they can come under the CSP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The other group will be for the matured PMETs made redundant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will waive the requirement on the six-month lead time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In other words, the moment they are retrenched, for those above 40 years old, they can apply to join CSP straight away without having to wait for six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Under the CSP, we are unable to promise same job, same pay.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: What we promise is our full support to help them find jobs as quickly as possible to start again at mid-career with a salary of at least $4,000, so that they can grow again from there.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are also helping more PMETs to switch careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: A lifelong career with the same company or even the same industry has become less likely for many people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mid-career PMETs may have to make a career change due to redundancy or other personal reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: That is the reason why we launched PCP in 2007, where we provide training and wage support up to 70% for the entire duration of training, which is typically about two years or less.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Since the launch in 2007, over 7,000 PMETs have benefited from this scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: One of them is Chong Kim Seng, 49 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He was not retrenched but he decided to make a career switch from electronics to biologics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Because Mr Chong looked at biologics as an emerging sector with tremendous potential.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There is a rising demand for medicines in Asian markets.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There is a good career progression path, where there is a headquarters operation, manufacturing or R&D in this sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He read in the public media that EDB has built up a healthy pipeline.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There are new plants as well as plant expansions over the next five years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In other words, this sector is going to grow in the next five years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There will be more jobs, there will more opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As a result, Mr Chong took a pay cut willingly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As I said, he was not retrenched, but he decided to take a pay cut to move from electronics to biologics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He has to take a pay cut because he did not have any prior experience relevant to the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He received a Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) Higher Certification in Process Technology and is now working as a Senior Quality Assurance specialist.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In fact, with his maturity and adaptability, I am very sure that he will find biologics a good career and one that will be good for him for the next 10 to 15 years and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 92 Dr Intan Mokhtar and Ms Thanaletchimi will be pleased to know that we are stepping up our efforts in the existing 10 PCP sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I think Ms Thanaletchimi will be very interested in this area.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This year, working together with MOH, we jointly launched added programmes for diagnostic radiographers, occupational therapists and physiotherapists.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In addition to that, we also recognise that some PMETs may not be switching careers from one sector to another, but they want to switch careers within the same sector, but different areas of specialisation within the same sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I think the point was brought up by Dr Intan Mokhtar.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Like in the case for ICT, there are now specialisations in areas of growing demand, such as cybersecurity, network administration, software development and other emerging jobs under the Smart Nation initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If Company A is downsizing, retrenching workers, Company B could be growing and expanding.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will support Company B to take over retrenched workers from Company A and help them go through the professional conversion, even at the company level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Another way to help mid-career PMETs is to match more of their expertise to the SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This was the point brought up by Mr Thomas Chua.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As mentioned by Mr Chua, many SMEs are growing and still hiring, but are looking for PMETs with experience and expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I was told that three areas of expertise are very popular and are in great demand by SMEs – business development, marketing and sales and operational management.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: They are looking for these types of people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: On the other hand, we also hear many mid-career PMETs say that they are not familiar with career opportunities with SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We launched P-Max just a year ago, to try out whether there is scope for us to connect the mid-career PMETs with the experience and expertise of interest to the SMEs, to connect them better.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She has 25 years of experience in operations, HR and administration with MNCs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She stopped work for one year to look after her mother.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Under P-Max, we matched her expertise to an SME.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She is now the HR and administration manager in an SME.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She is not alone; there are more than 800 of them under this programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are going to expand P-Max through more partners and more TACs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The schemes – that is, CSP, PCP, P-Max that I have covered so far – are targeted at the PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As brought up by Mr Chong Kee Hiong, we should not neglect the rank-and-file workers as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The rank-and-file jobseekers will, likewise, get more help under our Adapt and Grow programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We have a very successful Place-and-Train programme at NTUC e2i.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Typically, these trainings would last three to six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Last year, e2i, under the Place-and-Train programme, has placed 1,200 rank-and-file workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Soon, more sectors and programmes will be introduced this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We want to expand the outreach of this Place-and-Train programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For example, in the hotel sector, they are looking for Guest Services Officers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, we will put it under this programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In the infocomm media area, they are looking for communications and network associates, cybersecurity rank-and-file at the National ITE Certificate (NITEC) level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will include that under this Place-and-Train programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In addition to Place-and-Train, e2i and the career centres of WDA, also conduct career guidance, the one that Minister Ong Ye Kung mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We provide career guidance and every year, we conduct more than 200 job fairs to introduce more than 20,000 jobs to our jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Last year, we helped to place 11,000 rank-and-file workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mohd Fadzli, 30 years old, is one of them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He was working as a cleaner, earning $1,500.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He approached WDA Career Centre for career advice and guidance, so we guided him to move into the areas of Workplace Safety and Health (WSH).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: He went on to receive a WSQ Certificate in WSH, followed by a WSQ Advanced Certificate in WSH.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, he is working as a Safety Coordinator earning $2,200, a big increase from $1,500.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In some cases, when we try to match the rank-and-file workers to the jobs, both sides are unsure about each other.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The jobseekers are unsure about the job, and the employer is unsure about the worker.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For 80 hours, WDA will pay a token allowance to the person.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In other words, the employer does not have to pay anything.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: They work together for 80 hours just to try it out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: It is for the workers to try out the job, and for the employer to try out the worker.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: One example is Foo Lai Leng, 57 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She returned to work after 10 years, due to family commitments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She wanted to try out the early childhood sector, but she was not sure if this sector was suitable for her.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: After 80 hours, she decided that, yes, this is a career that she is interested in.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And yes, the companies in this sector also found her suitable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, she is working full-time as an Assistant Teacher.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: She is now going for a Diploma in Early Childhood Education as her next target.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We intend to help more and more jobseekers, for those who are unsure about what to do under this Work Trial programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: On the whole, for both rank-and-file workers and PMETs, we are stepping up efforts in employment facilitation for them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, besides workshops, seminars, recruitment events, job fairs, we are going to introduce e-services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For example, e2i is now trying out this Page: 94 concept of virtual job fairs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is a job fair but it does not happen in the real world; it is in the virtual world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: They help the jobseekers to submit not resumes, but "visume".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I asked them what is the difference between resumes and "visumes".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: What it means is that the e2i will help the jobseeker to do a video recording of how the person will describe himself, present his resume in a video form and they will send this video to the prospective employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The prospective employer will look at it over the virtual world, on the Internet.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Apparently, the response has been quite positive, so e2i intends to do more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: WDA, likewise, is going to introduce more e-career services, such as online matching, as well as online forum communities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will also improve our information support for both employers and the jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The National Jobs Bank does contain a lot of useful information, I think the point brought up by Assoc Prof Randolph Tan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Our challenge is how to do more data analytics to make that information more useful, more user-friendly, and enable jobseekers and employers to do more self-help, so that they can navigate the information themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Lastly, another area we will strengthen is our partnership with the employment agency (EA) industry.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This was a point brought up by Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are going to work with them closer to understand the current placement practices and to see how we can work with them, encourage or regulate the industry in such a way that they will step up and pay more attention to the placement of local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are going to partner the "best-in-class" placement companies, for example, those with industry specialisation or those who are jobseeker-centric.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are looking for a new model where the EAs have the incentive to become more jobseeker-centric.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: At the same time, we are looking for those with a strong network of employers because then, they will know where the job opportunities are.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In short, our second thrust is to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: First, sector by sector, through the SMPs to channel as many Singaporeans as we can into those respective sectors, to ensure that we have a strong Singapore Core in all the major sectors as we transform them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, enterprise by enterprise, individual by individual, through these career and employment support programmes that I described earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will do our very best to help out jobseekers, but we need our jobseekers to do their very best to help themselves too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: To my fellow Singaporeans, who are affected by redundancy, my concern for them is that the longer they are out of employment, the harder it will be for them to get back into employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We need them to do their best to help themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Be prepared to adapt to different jobs, if necessary, in different sectors and even different pay, so that they can grow again.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 95 Mdm Chair, our third and final thrust is to strengthen the global competitiveness of our Singapore Workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The Singapore Workforce today is made up of two-third locals and one-third foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As I had mentioned earlier, some have asked me, why not "Singaporean only", stop them from coming in and why not "Singaporean first"?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: They say, "Only when no Singaporean can do the job or want to do the job, then we allow them to come in".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I recall during my days with EDB, we walked the streets, we knocked on doors, we made cold calls, we made hot calls, we have tough calls, we have friendly calls.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Because quality investments are very hard to come by.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The better the investment, the stronger the competition, the stronger the competitors, the higher the demand of the investors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The toughest demand of all, for Singapore to meet, is not land or water, but manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
