text: We chased after wafer fabrication plants because we knew that consumer electronics, after a while, low value-added will be phased out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We knew that, one day, the disk drives sector will go through major restructuring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We needed to find a new growth sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Twenty years ago, we identified wafer fabrication industry as the next growth industry.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Each plant costs about US$1 billion to build.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Each plant is water-intensive and uses one million gallons of water every day.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, today, they are all supplied with NEWater.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But most importantly, each plant will need 1,000 workers – 500 PMETs and 500 production specialists.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Our local manpower is good, but we do not have enough, in terms of the range of expertise, experience and, most of all, the number.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As a result, we worked with these investors to borrow PMETs, to borrow workers from around the world, bring them into Singapore so that we can bridge three manpower gaps that we face − the number gap, the capability gap and the timing gap.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And I must say that this manpower strategy has worked very well for us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Yes, we have 2,000 foreign PMETs in these plants but, together with them, these 2,000 foreign PMETs, we are able to create jobs for 6,000 local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Looking back, if we had insisted on Singaporean Only, Singaporean First, I think these plants and many other good investments and good jobs would not be here today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, having foreign manpower in our Singapore workforce is a plus for us, not because Singaporeans are not good but because we simply do not have enough in the number, readiness and diversity of capabilities to meet the needs of the global investors and to beat the offers of the other global competitors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As we transform and grow into the future, we need to compete for even more, even better investments and we will have to face even bigger, even stronger competitors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The demands from investors will only get higher, especially on manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We stand a better chance of beating the competition, winning good investments and jobs if our local and foreign manpower here work together as one Singapore workforce − two-thirds plus one-third, as one Singapore workforce; rather than as two competing workforces − two-thirds versus one-third.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Because remember, two-thirds versus one-third will always be less than one.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: At the end of the day, we must recognise that Page: 96 the real competition is out there globally, not in here locally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, in other words, of all the jobs in Singapore today that pay more than $3,300, foreigners account for 21%, and locals 79%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: By sector, the foreigner share varies, of course, across industries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The highest is 37% in infocomm and F&B.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, these two sectors have the highest 37%, 38%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, from 32,000, it has dropped to 9,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Even though the overall ratio, both at the national and industry levels, shows that foreigners are a minority, just one-fifth at the national level and, with the exception of the two, infocomm and F&B, they are all less than one-third.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Yet, there is a perception among some Singaporeans that "Why am I a minority in my workplace, working here in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Why?" I think the answer is because of what I call the pockets of "EP concentration" in some companies, in some segments of the industry and at some locations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: These pockets of "EP concentration" have led to the perception of a liberal intake of EPs, which is not the case, or accusations of unfair consideration for locals or discrimination against our local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Currently, in processing EP applications, we assess only the individual-related criteria, that is, their qualification, experience and salary.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Going forward, we will also be looking at three additional factors that are "company-related".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, not just individual-related criteria but also company-related.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And the assessment will be carried out by Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The first assessment: how strong is the Singaporean Core in this company today?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The majority of the companies, as I mentioned earlier, in the same industry, have a healthy Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But there are outliers, significantly weaker than the industry norms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The second assessment: with a weak Singaporean Core today, do they have any firm commitment to nurture and strengthen the Singaporean Core for the future?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Thirdly, and finally, in consultation with relevant economic agencies, we will assess how relevant these "double weak" companies − that is, with weak in Singaporean Core and weak in commitment to nurture Singaporean Core – are to our economy and society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If they are not here, how much will we be affected?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And if the answer is not much, then they are what we call the "triple weak" companies − weak in Singaporean Core, weak in commitment and, at the same time, weak in economic linkage and social impact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Mr Patrick Tay has shared his concerns regarding these "triple weak" companies, which are our target for closer scrutiny.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If left unchecked, the sentiment of two-thirds Page: 97 versus one-third will continue to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: It will weaken the unity, cohesion and, eventually, the overall competitiveness of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: TAFEP is engaging them to improve their HR practices and will do a company-by-company review in six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So far, these firms have been broadly cooperative.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Some of them have acknowledged that there is room to strengthen the Singaporean Core, some have approached e2i/WDA to source for local PMETs through programmes, such as CSP and PCP, that I talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Some have engaged external help to review their internal HR process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Renewal of existing EPs, processing of new EP applications will be affected.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Curtailment of work pass privilege will have serious consequences on their continued operations and growth in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, we hope they will take corrective actions − move out of the "triple weak" list, do not just grow their business here but treat Singaporeans fairly, too, and help build a stronger Singaporean Core in their companies and industries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And I want to assure the vast majority of companies out there that they are not "triple weak" and, hence, will not be affected by this move.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: MOM will continue to serve them as per the current practice.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There is nothing to fear as long as they continue to treat our local PMETs fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As we take firm action against the "triple weak" companies, we will also take proactive action to recognise and partner those who are "triple strong" − strong in Singaporean Core, strong in commitment to nurture the Singaporean Core and strong in economic linkage or social impact, especially in sectors that are crucial to our future growth − Smart Nation, advanced manufacturing, future services and more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I am very encouraged and impressed by the few companies that I have visited so far.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: They believe in the development of human capital.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Yes, they tap on foreign PMETs to complement and strengthen their overall team and, yet, at the same time, they pay tremendous attention to value and nurture our local talents by transferring capability to them, giving them exposure and nurturing them for higher responsibility locally, regionally and globally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, in other words, instead of a mindset of two-thirds versus one-third, they embraced the mindset of two-thirds plus one-third.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And for some of them, two-thirds plus one-third can actually be bigger than one.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: To help strengthen the positive mindset of two-thirds plus one-third, we are going to grow this "triple strong" community.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are going to help them tap on SkillsFuture to strengthen the Singaporean Core at all levels in these "triple strong" companies: Earn and Learn at entry level; Mid-Career Enhancement; Leadership Development; and to provide greater facilitation for them to bring in foreign talents with the expertise to strengthen and transfer capability to our local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We can study some of the suggestions made by Mr Seah Kian Peng.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: One flagship initiative under the HCP is to nurture promising local talents into regional talents, into potential global talents and, tentatively, I intend to call this programme the "Glocal" Talent Development Programme. "Glocal" Talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Now, through this combination of efforts, countering the "triple weak", partnering the "triple strong", we want to send a clear signal and strong message that whether you are local or foreigner, whether employer or employee, whether you are union or management, we all have a role to play to work together to strengthen the Page: 98 Singapore workforce to compete for the best investments and jobs to Singapore for all to share.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: (In Mandarin):   During recent conversations with SME bosses, I asked them for their views on the current economic situation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Then I asked about their plans, and they said that since the outlook is uncertain, it is better to stay put.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Their view is that, if they do nothing, they will not make mistakes, so they will ride this out first and make plans later.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I am not a businessman, but through my interactions with business leaders in the past years, I have learnt a few things that are worth pondering over.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: It changes regardless of whether times are good or bad.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The difference is, when times are bad, changes are greater and they come faster.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The market may be quiet, but this is only what we see on the surface.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In reality, the market is undergoing swift changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is why, while it is quiet, it is the time to make changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Only through drastic changes and transformation, with a new look and new attitude, and by preparing well, can we face the future in a better shape.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In other words, so long as the enterprise has a clear and solid plan for transformation and is determined to persevere, MOM and various Government agencies will definitely give their full support and cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I hope SMEs can make good use of the LEDS programme to make big changes during the economic slowdown and not miss this good opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: With the changes taking place in the labour market, the business model of old is no longer relevant to the future economy. "After endless mountains and rivers that leave doubt whether there is a path out, suddenly one encounters the shade of a willow, bright flowers and a lovely village." Every cloud will have a silver lining.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If you run, I will run together with you; if you dash, I will dash together with you.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If more SMEs run together, the impetus will be stronger and the drive will be bigger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We can push and nudge one another and run towards this bright future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Singapore is not just an economy but a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Of course, we need to give our best to strengthen our economy through transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Only by doing so will we have enough resources for nation-building.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Amid this uncertainty, we will be more pro-business and try to attract the best investments and job opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 99﻿ However, we should not forget that the ultimate goal of economic development is to give opportunities for Singaporeans to fulfil their aspirations and ideals and to improve their quality of life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Therefore, not only do we need to be more pro-business, we also need to be more pro-worker, and help fellow Singaporeans constantly strive to better themselves, especially those impacted by the slowing economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will create new jobs for you and help you secure better job opportunities so as to strengthen our workforce with the Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: For workers who lose their jobs because of transformation, please do not lose heart.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will help you look for opportunities amidst this crisis, learn new skills and switch careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We will do our utmost to help you, but meanwhile, you must also do your best to help yourselves, for your own sake, and for the sake of your family.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, let us be determined and strive hard together, make every job a better job, make every worker a better worker and make every career an even better career.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Let us sprint forth towards the future economy and the future Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: (In English): Mdm Chair, I became an active member of Singapore Tripartism when I joined NTUC in 1996, 20 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: At that time, I learnt from then Secretary-General Brother Lim Boon Heng that a job is the best welfare for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Then, came the Asian Financial Crisis when we saw record retrenchments; I think about 29,000 workers lost their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Workers and union leaders became even more and more worried about the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, I decided to add one more line: a job is the best welfare and full employment is the best protection for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The positive employment outcomes which I outlined earlier and that we have today did not come easy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We actually made it happen here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In the Labour Movement, there is a strong spirit of solidarity because the Labour Movement always believes that unity is strength.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: And I believe that this spirit applies to the whole nation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We have major challenges to overcome, as I had outlined earlier, to transform to become more manpower-lean and productive, to build a stronger Singaporean Core and to strengthen the global competitiveness of the Singapore Workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Working in unity, whole-of-Government, whole-of-Tripartism, whole-of-Singapore, I believe we can succeed, and we must succeed to secure the best welfare – good jobs, good careers and the best protection, high employment, low unemployment – for our fellow workers, our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Page: 100 However, there are two key problems with existing schemes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While the Government has, in the implementation of FCF, recognised the existence of "double weak" firms, firms that are found to have flouted the rules will only have their work pass privileges curtailed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A second problem is the low take-up rates of voluntary schemes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: More can be done in pushing for an agenda in ensuring that the Singapore Core is able to contribute competitively but still ensure a competitive foreign labour force to be engaged by employers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This would unify all the current frameworks which loosely contribute to the Singapore Core drive into a single coherent framework to ensure minimal overlaps in policy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Even then, such a framework will take time to be debated and hammered out.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Transitional measures should be put in place to further the incentives for taking up fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I propose that a fair employment contribution fund where firms can contribute to help fair employment efforts.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In return, firms can enjoy incentives, such as corporate tax rebates or CPF employee credits.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The fund can be used to fund the agency overseeing any FCF activities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, SMEs are a vital part of our economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: However, our SMEs face challenges, such as tight labour market, difficulty in obtaining loans and an increasingly competitive environment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: More needs to be done to help SMEs stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The LEDS is a welcome initiative to help businesses adapt to a manpower-lean landscape and incentivise the development of a skilled Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: However, not many businesses seem ready or willing to take on this challenge.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry share what has been done so far under LEDS to encourage and support business transformation, and what more can be done, given the current business environment?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This is understandable as the rising level of non-performing loans last year was a problem for Singapore banks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: SMEs struggle to secure loans, some due to their short credit history and others due to a lack of collateral.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This lack of capital is stifling businesses and hampering innovation in our economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Will co-sharing of default risk change the bank's risk appetite in this business climate?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Since it is an equal sharing of risk, will Page: 101 there be an appeal process through MOM if SMEs could not obtain the loans from the banks?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: SMEs may also need smaller loans over shorter periods of time which banks may not be able to finance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is heartening to note that, recently, crowdfunding sites have sprung up to meet this need of matching individual investors with small companies that require funds.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The loans are more likely to be approved and are processed more quickly than at banks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: While this is good news for SMEs that need more funding, Singapore lacks specific guidelines for peer-to-peer lending.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, progressive workplace practices are essential to supporting our young families in pursuing the aspirations of raising a family and building a career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A young Singaporean, especially a new mother, requires a transition period after her maternity leave to adapt to a new work and childcare routine.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Especially for mothers who are breastfeeding, this transition period becomes even more critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A period of flexible work arrangements can help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During the Budget debate, my esteemed colleague, Mr Christopher de Souza supported my earlier call during the Debate on the President's Address to put in place eight weeks of FWAs on top of the 16 weeks of maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I support his bolder move of eight weeks of legislated right to unpaid maternity leave in view of FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These FWA options are important symbols of where we stand as a society in valuing people as our most important asset.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also accurately reflects the challenges faced by our mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also encourages our companies to seriously work towards providing FWAs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employees have the legal right to make a request in a reasonable manner for an FWA which can range from changes to hours, work patterns or locations of work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the UK, an employer can be taken to a tribunal if they do not handle the request in a reasonable manner and there is a good business reason to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we enhance the Grant to improve the take-up rate of FWAs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What other measures has the Ministry implemented or is planning to implement to extend the adoption of FWAs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Government and the Government-linked companies take the lead?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, we have the Tripartite Advisory on FWAs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry consider escalating the signature level and its support by turning it into tripartite guidelines of FWAs instead, to reflect its strong position in supporting young families?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the actual number of employees who utilise FWAs appears to be very low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Incentives are low and insufficient to encourage the utilisation of FWAs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current FWA set-up is entirely dependent on employers' voluntary initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After employees initiate such applications, employers can refuse a request on reasonable business grounds but must discuss options available with the employees, with the Ministry acting as facilitator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another thing that the Ministry could consider under the Work-Life Grant is to promote all roles flex for larger Singapore companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, PriceWaterhouse Coopers Australia extended flexible working to all 6,000 employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In all roles flex, employees' performance rather than actual face time and hours spent working becomes the most important criterion for work evaluation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Vesting employees such flexibility allows them to be at their best, fosters happy families so that employees can focus on their work and, therefore, positively impacts productivity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Chairman, with the increasing role that technology is having in both work and life, there is an opportunity to push for better integration of work and life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There is opportunity to leverage technology to allow for collaboration and productive work, allowing the focus on creativity and innovation, going beyond the mechanics of tasks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This, in turn, will raise productivity for organisations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As we talk about innovation and the need to restructure, I believe that we should also be open-minded to new models for work, rather than just thinking of providing FWAs for both small and large organisations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In fact, especially for smaller organisations, where resources are scarce, companies should innovate on how work is done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The use of technology alone, however, is not sufficient.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There must also be relevant changes to work processes, HR and performance policy to enable quality work to be done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Just imagine how much time can be saved if people are equipped and allowed to work from wherever they are.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: When a professional completes a meeting with a client at the client's office, he is able to access the relevant information he requires via whatever device he carries, to go and prepare for his next meeting with his colleagues from any suitable location in the client's office or to go to a site nearby.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Just imagine how much time he saves as there is no need for travel time in terms of the effort to return to the office before being able to have his next meeting.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Just think about how much time that could also be saved or be released to do work which is needed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This changes the whole concept of allowing people to do their best work from wherever they are, made possible by leveraging the right technology to enable a quality work experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For flexible work to be made available should be a benefit made to all, so that it changes the whole work culture and you do not single out a particular group, and that people can, therefore, work and access the kind of work and information they need for quality work experience and clear outcomes and impact.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, general HR knowledge may not be enough for these professionals to add strategic value to companies, industries and the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For that to happen, they must also acquire knowledge, hone skills and gain experience in the context of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are three key realities that HR practitioners in Singapore must know and be familiar with.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have spoken at length in my maiden speech in this House on the unusual tripartite partnership in Singapore and how it serves as a key economic advantage for us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second is a local workforce that is maturing and soon peaking in numbers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The third is how to ensure a Singaporean Core within a nationality-diverse workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Until and unless there is a deep and proper understanding of these realities and the design of methods to help companies do well in this context, the HR function will not be able to advance beyond a tactical and administrative role.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Looking back, I am happy to note that the Government has shown great support in working with the Labour Movement and our Tripartite Partners to embark on breakthrough initiatives, such as the Progressive Wage Model, NTUC U Care Centre, Best Sourcing, the Inclusive Growth Programme (IGP) and others, to help low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are definitely moving in the right direction to become a more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The importance of these initiatives cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All these efforts have resulted in better wages and working conditions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But we still have a long way to go.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For several of our low-wage workers in Singapore, these initiatives provide hope at improving their livelihoods and hopes for a better future for their families.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my Budget Debate speech, I suggested that we set a target to have a higher real wage increase for our workers at the 20th percentile, compared to the median.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will MOM, perhaps working together with other relevant Ministries like MOF, consider setting such a target?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also made a suggestion of mandating Annual Wage Supplements (AWS) and Annual Increments as part of the licensing condition for the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This may be a more practical approach in helping low-wage workers, compared to mandating compliance with the National Wages Council's recommendations targeted at them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government can also explore supporting job redesign initiatives to ensure alignment with SkillsFuture, so that workers can apply the skills they have acquired to improve their productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there plans to expand the scope of support provided to this group of vulnerable workers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, in the last few years, the Government has introduced various schemes and initiatives to help low-wage workers, including Workfare and the WorkRight Initiative.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It has also worked with Tripartite Partners to develop and implement the Progressive Wage Model in certain low-wage sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In the event that this group of workers lose their jobs, what kind of support does MOM provide to these vulnerable workers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: When companies downsize and close down, MOM should make it a requirement for the companies to direct the displaced employees to WDA, so that the Government can assist them through the various schemes and resources, such as the National Jobs Bank, CSP and PCP.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Retrenched employees may not be aware of or are too shy to go for such help, but if this forms part of the retrenchment programme of the company, it will have more outreach.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The National Jobs Bank has a number of jobs in low-wage sectors, but many low-wage workers will need help to access this website.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Others do not have computers or Internet connection.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would MOM consider setting up physical National Jobs Bank pop-up booths at accessible locations, such as MRT stations or community centres?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: WDA runs a number of job and career support programmes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the effectiveness of and the challenges faced by these schemes?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: For retrenched PMETs faced with structural unemployment, is there scope to increase the number of PCPs to help them find jobs in growth sectors?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Currently, Special Employment Credit is given to companies that hire older workers.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: To encourage companies to continue the employment of its existing older workers, would the Ministry consider extending a scheme similar to Special Employment Credit for these companies?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We should also provide more work options for older workers and retirees who want to work shorter hours or flexi-time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: So far, FWAs are not very common in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Government work with the TACs to assist companies in redesigning workflows to allow for more FWAs, so that it will become more widely adopted?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Not only will this help to improve the work-life balance nationwide, but it will also enable more mothers, older or retired workers to participate in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry share with us how widely have FWAs been adopted within the Civil Service and Government agencies?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I would also like to know the form these arrangements take and the profiles of the involved staff in terms of job functions, seniority, gender and duration of the FWAs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Ministry have any quantifiable targets and deadlines for the percentage of workplaces which offer FWAs?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: How does Singapore compare with other developed nations in this respect?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: These would be good benchmarks for private companies to follow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Unfortunately, we continue to experience workplace fatalities where workers die due to workplace accidents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: These workplace fatalities included the two young lives which were lost in a tragic accident on the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) tracks near Pasir Ris MRT station just last month.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: These numbers are truly alarming and beg for immediate attention.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: We must prevent the occurrence of workplace accidents and these accidents can be prevented.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: We simply cannot take workplace safety for granted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can MOM share how it intends to work with the tripartite partners to strengthen and enforce workplace safety measures across all industries?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can MOM do more to encourage and support our SMEs in accessing and managing workplace safety more effectively?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, as mentioned in my Budget Debate speech, I believe the Government should put in more effort to track under-employment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the Government could put into its headline numbers not just the employment and unemployment rates but two other indicators it is already gathering.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Headlining time-related underemployment and the number of discouraged workers will focus public attention on these two important statistics that are not captured in the employment and unemployment headlines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How can we measure underemployment where a person is being underutilised in terms of his earning capacity?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could we consider collecting data on income earned versus median income for that qualification and age, or perhaps compared with previous income?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, it has been noted in the US that in the last decade, the growth of temporary and contract jobs has surged, with the proportion of Americans working as independent contractors soaring.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can we expect such alternative work arrangements to increase, given the uncertain economy, the need for employers to manage costs and the automation of jobs?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If so, there will be more Singaporeans facing issues, such as poor job security, intermittent Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions and little or no medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, today, I must say I have learnt a lot from Minister Lim Swee Say.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: There are so many terms – PCP, CSP, LEDS.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: For me, in my line of Page: 106 work, LED means light-emitting diodes, but yours is a bit different.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister have shared a lot about PMEs and I am really, really glad that so many things have happened.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, I would like to express my concern about the PME group, especially after doing a lot of community work for the last 13 years.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Those in the middle-aged category who are skilled and possess tertiary educational qualifications, generally struggle to be re-employed after being retrenched.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This meant that roughly half of the older PMEs could not find a job within six months of being laid off, let alone finding one of comparable grade and salary.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is worrisome that 77% of the PMEs looking for re-employment were aged 40 and above.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Losing one's job through retrenchment can be a devastating, if not traumatic, experience.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The affected worker may lose his or her self-esteem and self-confidence.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It could lead to health issues when one's mental state is not at rest.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to qualify that I appreciate all these safety nets that MOM has put in place.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What I am going to propose here is not to undermine what has been done, but I thought it would complement the whole safety net framework.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: TIS is for those who have lost their job due to retrenchment, resulting in an immediate loss of income.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is meant to cushion the impact, providing continuity to their daily life and mitigating potential disruption to their children's educational progress and the well-being of their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed scheme is progressively decreasing in nature, that is, the payout is calibrated downwards towards zero at the end of a four-month period after being laid off.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: For the first month, he/she receives 75% of his/her last drawn salary.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In the second and third month, it is 50% of his/her last drawn salary and, the fourth month, which is the final month, it is 25% of his/her last drawn salary.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Knowing it is going to go down, it will give him the urgency to find a new job.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The last drawn salary is capped at $6,000.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, we can discuss further the details.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: During the four-month period, the worker is encouraged to take up new skills to help him/her gain re-employment.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Upon re- employment, the TIS scheme will be terminated automatically.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, the scheme will lapse after four months, even if the worker has not gained any employment.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is just a temporary cushion given to the worker.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The usage of CPF contributions towards this TIS scheme is just an expansion to its purpose to supplement the workers in times of dire need, such as medical, housing, education, retirement and, in this case, unforeseeable loss of income.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I acknowledge that this idea is not a new one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: It is similar to others which have been raised before.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like I mentioned in my speech in the Budget Debate, as the old economy gets replaced by a new one, job redundancy and obsolescence are inevitable.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I salute the Government for taking proactive and constructive measures for our workers through retraining and reskilling.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we should continue to explore all possibilities, especially so when I reckon this issue will be with us for many more years to come.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I also believe it is going to get tougher with each passing year.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Azmoon, your suggestion is very interesting, but I am afraid you have run out of time.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad
text: I think we can study further if you need more information.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will be especially helpful to many women who "work" at home as the primary caregiver of their families, with no paid wages and little retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, this is going to be very helpful to them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Taken together with the slew of enhancements made to CPF in 2015, the scheme is now more attractive, more comprehensive and better catered to the diverse needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, how much does the average Singaporean understand of the CPF scheme in order to fully leverage its benefits?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Other than a small group of financially-savvy individuals, it is not easy for most of us to remember the different tiers of interest rates offered in the different accounts, as well as the different rules that apply, so that we can optimise our own savings and those of our family members.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I would admit that this will not be an easy task, given the complexity of the system.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, we should consider some learnings from the field of behavioural finance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Drawing on the research of psychology of decision-making, behavioural finance argues that many financial phenomena are the result of less than fully rational thinking on the part of the participants.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Behavioural finance helps explain sub-optimal trading and investment behaviours.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The science of behavioural finance is already applied to understand asset pricing, investor behaviour and corporate finance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: MOM should study carefully the patterns of transaction of CPF members and take a very proactive role to help members to fully optimise the benefits of the CPF scheme.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, since January 2016, CPF members can transfer CPF savings above the Basic Retirement Sum to their spouse's Special Retirement Account instead of the previous Full Retirement Sum.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This change means couples stand to benefit significantly if they have varying levels of CPF savings between them.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I believe that even though it is still early days, as it was just implemented, thus far, very few CPF members whom I have spoken to have thought about this, let alone take action to enhance their savings in this way.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: CPF members who do not wish to participate can opt out.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But they should be helped by a statement explaining how much less they will get as a couple if they do so.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This approach may help result in more couples benefiting from the extra interest rates, which will be particularly welcome for lower balances.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must do our very best to ensure all Singaporeans can take full advantage of it.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The payouts are meant to provide a modest but meaningful supplement to their retirement incomes in support of the bottom 20% to 30% of Singaporean seniors.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: With monthly payouts and a more consistent liquidity that they provide, the elderly will be better able to manage their day-to-day expenses.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Would behavioural economics suggest that making the payouts monthly could even nurture the seniors to use more of the payouts to pay for those significant living expenses that are incurred monthly, such as utility bills and others?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As Members have said in many different ways, I hope that a degree of flexibility can be built into the eligibility considerations of the payout scheme involving the three criteria of lifetime wages, housing types and household support.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate that clear-cut rules and a high degree of administrative efficiency may be required to deliver Silver Support to needy seniors in large enough numbers.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: However, balanced against that consideration is, of course, our hope that specific needy seniors who deserve support do not fall through the cracks of rigid eligibility criteria.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Chen, I am sorry, you have also run out of time.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao
text: Some use of resources, time and effort in making discretionary assessments in exceptional cases would be well-spent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To address the multifaceted problems they face, we need holistic and cross-disciplinary solutions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may be a task too large for any one body to take up on its own.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our universities and members of civil society who have worked with migrant workers are sources of information and practical expertise that could be a brain trust for the Government.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that with greater collaboration among the different stakeholders in the sector, we can show that Singapore also cares for and about the workers who have contributed to our nation-building.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Mr Chairman, I am addressing the House about LEDS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The economic environment situation is getting very real, so we have mentioned that there will be structural labour market challenges, such as slower workforce growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But there are also other challenges, such as external economic macro challenges, whether it is the US undergoing an economic recovery or China slowing its growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: There are also security issues around the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We should also not forget that technology has advanced to the extent where startups are posing threats to traditional businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, we hear a lot about disruptive technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But more importantly, in fact, across the world, we are all facing productivity challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Productivity growth has challenged us and Singapore has to punch above its weight in order to ride to economic success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Companies are faced with this issue, especially SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: That is why we need SMEs to review and know what they need to do to enhance their processes to enable themselves to compete in the marketplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We need to make sure that we have an ecosystem and environment for SMEs to grow and help progressive businesses to undergo transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We hope that these companies, especially SMEs, which comprise more than 90% of our registered entities, will continue to build a Singaporean Core in a very manpower-lean economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: If it is going to be manpower-lean, companies will have to learn to survive in this very manpower-lean economy by being lean themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Late last year, Minister Lim Swee Say launched the LED concept.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is a pro-business and pro-worker concept at the same time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: I was in MTI for five years working on productivity schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Applications for productivity schemes continue to go up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The question we ask ourselves is: why is the productivity index not going up as well?

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Productivity schemes and grants cover a wide area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, many companies apply for productivity schemes and grants and they get the grants but the change is not comprehensive enough to attain a productivity Page: 110 movement or a lean manpower outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: When I understood what the LED concept was about and the vision of what Minister Lim wanted to do, I thought: "This programme would build depth." It would require the firms to dig deep into their companies to look at the processes that they have and see what changes they would have to make, before they could start thinking about what productivity schemes or grants can be put in place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: From concept, we developed it into a scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Chairman, with your permission, I have asked the Clerks to place a handout, entitled "LED Scheme – Integrated Support", on the hon Members' seats during the tea break.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: If we achieve the three objectives mentioned above, we are going to be future-ready.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is about helping companies to become more manpower-lean and more productive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Over the last few days, in this House, many people used sports analogies, from marathons to high performance sports.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: I want to use these as well, since I am a very passionate sportsman.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: In the LEDS, it is really like weightlifting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: You see some weightlifters are lighter but they can lift as much as those who are heavier in weight.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: By right, if you are heavier, you are supposed to lift more or lift the same weight.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But some of them who are thin, they can lift the same.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This is what we call the power-to-weight ratio.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: If the power-to-weight ratio is high, you are super fit and super strong.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: If your power-to-weight ratio is one-to-one, then you can only lift your own weight, and that is average.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We want the lean companies or manpower-lean companies to attain high power-to-weight ratio, and that would mean to punch above their weight.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: To achieve that, they have to undergo three phases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: These three phases, simply put, include the current state of the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Then their business processes will go through a transition of two years – with automation, productivity, process change, job redesign, putting in computerisation and changing the workforce composition in order to achieve the future state.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: These three phases will need to be supported by the agencies, policies and Government schemes as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, we are going to help SMEs undergo these three phases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We will assess all the proposals and see whether their proposals for productivity and being manpower-lean could really result in meaningful change within, say, two years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, businesses do not need to worry about what schemes and what productivity grants to apply for.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: As long as they have the intent to become more manpower-lean, and they apply and are approved as an LED-supported company, we will help to coordinate all the different Government schemes needed for it to succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: These foreign employees can then impart their skills and knowledge to our local workforce, so that locals can be upskilled and take on better jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This temporary foreign manpower flexibility can then be withdrawn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is not an easy process, but definitely achievable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Based on the applications that I have received so far, it is quite promising.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We need the arms and legs and we need the Page: 111 partnership of TACs to help us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: They include the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry and NTUC's U-SME.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The LED multipliers will educate and handhold companies in the whole application process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: SMEs need not worry about whom to approach, because they can approach any of these 10 multipliers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Even the SME Centres, SMEs can approach them and the SME Centres will guide them through the process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So far, the LED multipliers have held four road shows, and I have participated in all of them, and we would want to continue to build up this outreach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: To date, all the 10 multipliers have plans to engage their members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We are going to link up these 10 LED multipliers, not just with business advisors, but also consultants who are professionals in productivity as well as manpower-lean strategies and processes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: I am glad to see that the Member Mr Lee Yi Shyan has mentioned F&B.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: There will be a fair bit of transformation in that sector if more come forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: There are also many who apply for other grants but achieve manpower-lean outcomes without needing temporary foreign worker flexibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We have more than 200 companies in that category.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, there is hope for higher productivity moving forward, because there is greater depth now in terms of their transformation and process change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We have studied all the applications and proposals and we found that there are three commonalties in this whole development and in their proposals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: First, they centralise a lot of their operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: What this means is that they share facilities among groups of companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We have more than 10 companies coming forward and saying, "Let us come together, take our basic processes and centralise them", thereby achieving some economies of scale and reducing wastage and then, through a hub-and-spoke kind of network, they could do their own differentiation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This automation plan helps them to combine man and machine, as well as to put in machinery within a business process or operational process to make it more efficient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: They also support job redesign and reduce lots of manpower wastage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Thirdly and most importantly, they develop new skillsets or enhance the skill development, especially for our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This imparting of new skills will align to our SkillsFuture vision and mission to enable locals to take on new types of jobs in future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, if the company changes, the worker's job changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: A good example comes from the Indian Restaurants Association (Singapore).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Fourteen members of the Association collaborated to form a consortium.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: You are probably wondering how they can come together because they could be competitors as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But they could, because they felt that there were some basic processes that were the same and they could consolidate them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Page: 112 So, firstly, they achieved the objective of centralising shared services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The consortium will form a central processing unit or a shared kitchen, where the basic processes will be centralised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Basic processes involve preparing the certain basic ingredients – onions, cabbage, vegetables and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Subsequently, these will be delivered to the restaurants' individual kitchens for their own recipe so that they will prepare the dishes differently.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: For some, automation will be done in their individual restaurants, in their individual kitchens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The skills transfer is extremely important because they are building a sustainable pipeline of local Indian cuisine chefs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is not easy to achieve such a manpower-lean state and we are still going through the process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But we saw a lot of progress and we want to work by sectors, clusters and individual companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: I fully agree with Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Mr Lee Yi Shyan and Mr Thomas Chua that more should be done to help more businesses to break these barriers and shift mindsets in order to achieve this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: You have to think out of the box, change your mindsets to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But it takes the whole-of-Government as well to support such a transformation programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This year's Budget has got a lot to do with Industry Transformation Programmes and LEDS plays its part to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: LEDS also depends on good HR practices, and good HR practices require good HR and qualified HR professionals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: In managing manpower and the workforce in a company, it has to go beyond HR or human resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is not just human resource but human capital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: There is a difference here, especially in the way we plan, and in managing the human resource within the company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: HR is not just about plugging holes – when there is a job vacancy, you find a suitable person, you plug a hole here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: A lot of times they are faced with situations which extend beyond recruitment, with retention, for example.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We need a strategic and longer term plan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Look at every single individual, not just as a factor of production, but as capital for investment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Invest in them early, even for our mature workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: As Mr Thomas Chua has pointed out, companies will need to focus more on building and nurturing human capital, investing in identifying each employee's strengths and making the best use of differentiated talents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We have many good examples that did that, and many are SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Sometimes, it is not about investing only in the young but investing across the board – young and old.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: ROHEI Corporation, a local corporate training SME consultancy, is one such SME.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: They advocate "people above process", often going out of their way to nurture and guide their employees towards achieving their life goals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: When their senior consultants in their 50s expressed interest to master different skillsets and practices offered by the business, the company readily supported and guided them to acquire those skills, even though they were close to retirement age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: They wanted to ensure that their wisdom and skills could combine together to help the company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This ensured that they could continue to value add, even in Page: 113 their golden years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Every single person counts, they are our capital, they are our assets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But you need a good HR practitioner if you want to implement such a process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: All HR practitioners now have more demanding jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: To upgrade the HR practices in the different sectors, we need to upgrade their learning process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Mr Melvin Yong has asked for an update.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: One recurring feedback is that they felt the need for HR to evolve to better support business strategy and to be more strategic, to think in the longer term and to be able to look at the macro view of the company; basically, to think like a chief executive officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: They have to move from focusing on operational and transactional approaches, to a more strategic approach, to look at how the company moves forward, forecast its manpower needs in the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Employers expect that HR professionals can better apply these skills and align them to the organisation's goals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The HR strategy has to be integrated within the company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The committee is also recommending that we develop a pathway because of that requirement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We are looking at setting up a system to certify HR professionals based on components, such as HR competencies, HR work experience, professional code of conduct and ethics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Also, they have to possess an understanding of local employment laws, regulations and practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is a progressive learning ladder as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: This framework has to provide the HR professionals with a comprehensive roadmap to develop their own capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: They need to advance their careers through that.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: HR professionals, once they have gone through the process, can then better support businesses and also enhance their value to the organisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The work of the HR professionals has become more demanding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: As the expectations increase from bosses to workers to everybody, sometimes, they are sandwiched in the middle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Many times, the expectation from the workers or the employees is about the work-to-personal time ratio.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: As Ms Jessica Tan had mentioned, how do you integrate that work and that life together?

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: It is not easy to find that integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: And it is a very critical component and critical success factor for any good company that wants to retain its staff, wants to keep it more dynamic and also wants to recruit personnel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Ms Jessica Tan is right to highlight that FWAs can help businesses thrive, leveraging technology to do so, enhancing it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: For example, hotdesking, working from home, working from any other place – it is a flexible workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We know that the majority of global businesses have reported increases in employee productivity and company revenue as a result of implementing Page: 114 FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: I agree with Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Desmond Choo that more should be done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The Tripartite Committee on Work-Life Strategy (TriCom), which includes representatives from trade associations, has launched several initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The Tripartite Advisory on FWAs was launched in November 2014 to help employers, supervisors and employees through the journey of implementing FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But more efforts in awareness and education are needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: So, we rolled out the Work-Life campaign, which concluded in March 2016, to reinforce that FWAs would benefit both employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Moving forward, we will take a more targeted approach towards some of the sectors that are facing challenges to adopt the FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We note Mr Desmond Choo and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh have asked about Work-Life Grant adoption rates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: In particular, the take-up rate of the Developmental Grant, which defrays the cost of companies on a pilot scheme, is increasing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Mr Desmond Choo has asked about the Government's stance on legislating FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: The success of it depends on integration of different factors, for example, the perception of such a practice within the society, and employers' and co-workers' attitudes towards FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: In other countries, FWAs are usually fairly prevalent before this legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: That will not stop us from taking a review as well as making sure that we continue the awareness and education campaign.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Fundamentally, employers and employees need to understand and be committed before such a culture can be in place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Chairman, a large part of this Budget is about helping SMEs in the industry, and our workforce to adapt and grow for better jobs and better careers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We rolled out so many different schemes – LEDS, LEDS Multipliers, HR certification and HR/HC, the Work-Life Grant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Most importantly, mindsets need to shift for SMEs need to have the spirit of enterprise to make the change, take that leap of faith and take action on it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: We are left with the SMEs to help themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: Transformation is not easy, but nothing comes easy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Teo Ser Luck)
text: But if we put our hearts and minds together, I am sure we can build and ride the fourth wave of economic success towards the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Mr Chairman, I will now brief the House on three of MOM's focus areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: One, is to help older workers remain employable; two, is to improve low-wage workers' earnings; and three, is to improve workplace safety and Page: 115 health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Allow me to, first, touch on older workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This trend will continue over the next two decades and we must be prepared to accept and embrace this new reality and turn it into opportunity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: The Government has been engaging Singaporeans of all ages on various platforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: One common feedback that we hear is that seniors want to have meaningful jobs that tap on their wealth of experience and resources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: But the responsibility for creating a sustainable working environment for older workers does not just lie with the Government alone, although the Government can take a lead in this area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: My Ministry has, therefore, been working closely with the tripartite partners to help older workers, under the Tripartite Committee on Employability of Older Workers, or Tricom in short.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: The Tricom, which I chair, has introduced a series of initiatives to help older workers work for as long as they are willing and able to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We have made some encouraging progress in this direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is well above the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) average of 57% and is comparable with some of the developed and advanced countries like Japan's 70% and South Korea's 66%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Notwithstanding this encouraging process, I share Mr Chong Kee Hiong's view that more has to be done to encourage the hiring of older workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: However, we cannot achieve this goal by giving incentives alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: For there to be a truly age-friendly workplace, mindsets must be changed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: The nature and the design of the jobs must also be changed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: To change mindsets, Tricom works through the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) to champion positive workplace attitudes towards older workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: TAFEP has been conducting ongoing publicity campaigns to emphasise the value that older workers can bring to companies and their younger co-workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
