text: To change the nature of jobs and the working environment, we need to support employers to adopt good age management practices and redesign job processes for their older workers, a point highlighted by Mr Chong Kee Hiong.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We have been providing our support through the Workpro grants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: To further enhance the effectiveness of the Workpro scheme, MOM and WDA are in the process of reviewing this scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: I wish to take this opportunity to strongly encourage more employers to make use of the enhanced Workpro grants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In the early years, older workers were less wage-competitive because of rigid seniority-based wages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: When the minimum retirement age was raised to 62 in 1999, the tripartite partners at that time agreed that the law could provide some flexibility for employers to reduce the wages of workers turning 60 by up to 10%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Since then, the tripartite partners have worked hard to promote flexible and performance-based wage systems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: So, the wage-cut provision that was put in place in 1999 is no longer relevant Page: 116 today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Going forward, pay should be reflective of workers' job scope and value, rather than their age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Four years since we introduced the re-employment concept, I am pleased to say that implementation of this scheme has been relatively smooth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In recent years, over 98% of local employees who wished to continue working were offered employment beyond 62.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: When we introduced re-employment in 2012, we also committed to raising the re-employment age from 65 to 67 at an appropriate time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is to help smoothen the transitional process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Even as we work towards raising the re-employment age, the Tricom has considered other ways to expand re-employment options for employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We have received feedback that, sometimes, employers are unable to find suitable jobs in their own companies, but can help the worker secure re-employment in a related or subsidiary company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: As with the other changes announced earlier, this will also take effect on 1 July 2017.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: The tripartite partners strongly agree that employers should consider all available re-employment options to identify suitable jobs for their employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: However, there will be situations where re-employment is just simply genuinely not possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: As a last resort, we have provided for an Employment Assistance Payment (EAP).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Taken together, all these measures mentioned earlier, represent significant changes for our re-employment landscape.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: To better prepare employers and their workers, the Tricom has updated the Tripartite Guidelines on Re-employment of Older Employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: It will provide details on many of the changes that I spoke on earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We will be releasing these guidelines in the next few weeks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is especially important, given our tight labour market in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: I will now turn to the second issue – low-wage workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari has asked for an update on the measures the Government has taken in this area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: They are Workfare and the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: The Workfare Training Support (WTS) scheme Page: 117 also provides significant support to low-wage workers to upgrade their skills so they can stay employable and enjoy higher wage growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In specific sectors with a larger concentration of low-wage workers, prevalent cheap-sourcing was causing wages to stagnate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: To address this concern, we set up tripartite committees to develop PWMs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is something that Mr Zainal Sapari is very familiar with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: These PWMs provide cleaners, security officers and landscape workers with a clear pathway of career progression.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: The workers can look forward to earning higher wages, in line with higher skills and productivity improvements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We will implement PWMs for the landscape and security industries through Government levers from 30 June and 1 September this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We are encouraged by the early PWM adopters in the security and landscape industries which have already sent their workers for the requisite training and they are also already paying them according to the PWM model.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We strongly urge the remaining employers to expedite their plans to meet the PWM requirements, so that more workers can benefit from the higher skills and better wages and their employers can also benefit from workers' higher productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari has proposed mandating annual wage supplements and annual increments for low-wage workers in the cleaning, security and landscape sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is a major proposal which will not only affect workers' well-being, but also employers and the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: It is, therefore, crucial to seek the views of the various stakeholders in the usual spirit of tripartism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We will raise Mr Zainal's suggestion to the tripartite committees responsible for the PWMs for these sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: And the tripartite partners will need to decide on what is appropriate and feasible, taking into consideration the interest of workers and bearing in mind economic conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is comparable with the growth in the median incomes over the same period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We will continue to work very closely with our tripartite partners on this important issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Before I move on to my next subject, I would also like to address Mr Patrick Tay's point on freelancers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Freelancers are not covered by the Employment Act and the Work Injury Compensation Act (WICA) because there is no employer-employee relationship between them and their clients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is a complex issue which we should study carefully and not rush into.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In the meantime, we will support efforts like those from the NTUC's Freelancers and Self-Employed Unit which has different initiatives for different groups of freelancers, ranging from taxi drivers to those in the creative and media sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is in recognition that freelancers are a diverse group comprising Page: 118 many different trades, skills, values and services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: It is, therefore, difficult to prescribe a one-size-fits-all solution to address such diverse and complex needs and situations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In 2015, our workplace fatality rate was 1.9 fatalities per 100,000 employed persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is a slight increase from 1.8 in 2014.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Although the increase is quite marginal but we are concerned, nonetheless.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Just this year alone, we lost 22 lives at work, as mentioned by Mr Melvin Yong just now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In fact, personally, to me, every one fatality is just one too many.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Therefore, I agree with Mr Melvin Yong and Ms Thanaletchimi that more needs to be done to raise our WSH standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We will adopt a four-pronged approach to reduce the workplace fatality and incident rate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: First, we will raise awareness; second, we will build WSH capability; third, we will strengthen enforcement; and, lastly, we will impose heavier penalties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: My Ministry has put in a large amount of effort over the years to raise WSH awareness among workers, employers and the general public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: To build WSH capability, we work closely with the industry to assist them in bringing good WSH practices to their workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In terms of enforcement, we conduct around 16,000 workplace inspections a year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: That is more than 1,300 inspections every month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: In the last few months, I have personally participated in three inspections, and I will continue to do so until I feel that the level of workplace safety reaches a satisfactory level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: To strengthen deterrence, my Ministry will also be taking tougher actions against recalcitrant employers and will impose harsher penalties if things do not improve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Fundamentally, WSH needs to be driven from the top.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: At the very top, we want industry leaders to set the tone and be committed to WSH.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: My message to them is a simple and sincere one.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: That is, my Ministry is always ready to work together with the industry to improve safety standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We are doing this as a last resort as we have the responsibility to protect our workers to ensure that they work in a safe and healthy environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: More details on the WSH capability building programme will be announced later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Minister Lim Swee Say will now address the remaining issues in his round-up speech.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Chairman, please allow me to address some of the other cuts put up by the Members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will be introducing a new Bill later this year, which will include the necessary changes related to the Act that Mr Patrick Tay spoke of, to implement these changes.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, if a company is perceived to have adopted unfair practices, especially discrimination based on nationality, we will investigate.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If found to be substantiated, the company is subjected to additional scrutiny, like those that I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On TAFEP, Mr Faisal Manap raised the need to strengthen the framework for workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Currently, the arrangement is that TAFEP and MOM work together to promote fair employment as well as address discrimination in terms of whatever practices that we come across.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The arrangement is that the tripartite partner, through TAFEP, will do the promotion work whereas the enforcement will be through MOM.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, TAFEP, upon their promotion and investigation, if they come across any organisation which, in their view, has adopted the unfair practices, TAFEP will alert MOM and then we will take the enforcement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: TAFEP's finding or assessment carries a lot of weight with MOM.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So far, the employers approached by TAFEP have mostly heeded the advice by TAFEP and made adjustments to their employment practices.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Earlier, I mentioned about the "triple weak" and "triple strong".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, that will be another avenue for TAFEP to step up the effort not just in terms of promotion but advocacy as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Along with the unemployment figures, statistics on time-related underemployment and discouraged workers are also published annually, every year, in the Report on Labour Force in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The last report was released in January 2016.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What is even more encouraging is that it is on the decline.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, for example, in 2013, it was more than 4%, then in 2014, it went below 4% and last year, 2015, it went below 3%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This has to do with the tight labour market that we face today.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As mentioned by Ms Sylvia Lim, time-related underemployment is the only internationally accepted statistical definition of underemployment and it is recommended by the International Labour Organization, so we comply with that.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As regards the share of discouraged workers in the resident workforce in 2015, it was stable and low at 0.4%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the issue of contract workers and freelancers, Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether they are on the increase, whether they reflect a rise in underemployment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The percentage of workers on contract, that means they are working as employees but on contract, has dropped from 12.7% in 2009 to Page: 120 11.3% last year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of freelancers, they are what we call the "own account" holders, so they are like self-employed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That percentage of the workforce has dropped from 9.2% to 7.9% over the same period, from 2009 to 2015.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, both employees on contract as well as freelancers as a percentage of the workforce have been on the decline.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The question is whether they choose to be in this situation − contract or freelancer, or they are forced to be in this position.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the part of MOM, what we are trying to do our best is that we offer them options.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, if they feel that they do not want to continue with their contract work or be freelancers, I hope they will step forward, take advantage of our CSP, PCP, P-Max and all the other programmes that I talked about earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the issue of unemployment insurance raised by Mr Azmoon, first of all, let me make it clear that I do sympathise and empathise with workers who are affected by retrenchments and I appreciate the suggestions by various Members, including Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Patrick Tay, for unemployment benefits or insurance schemes to help cushion the impact on such workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As I mentioned earlier, our situation in Singapore is quite different from the situation in most of these other countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our unemployment rates are low and our long-term unemployment rates are also low.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, and this is something that is worth taking note, the practice of paying retrenchment benefits in Singapore is widespread.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is a fairly standard practice in the industries and in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is the reason why MOM is focusing our efforts on helping retrenched workers to go back to work as quickly as possible because unemployment is low, under-employment is low, long-term unemployment is low and there is a widespread practice of paying retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The top priority for many workers is to go back to work.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is the reason why, earlier, I spent a lot of time going into a lot of details to explain the kind of options that we are offering to our workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I hope that more of them can tap on the programmes that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Azmoon suggested that one way is to allow workers to tap on the CPF savings to finance such schemes like TIS.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: My reservation is that today, CPF is already used to meet housing, education, healthcare and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we should be very careful not to deplete these savings further by using them for other purposes unless it is really necessary to do so.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For now, let us focus in helping the unemployed workers to go back to work.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about retrenchment benefits and whether we can introduce compulsory retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The tripartite partners have discussed this from time to time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is because the different retrenching companies are in different circumstances and therefore, it cannot be a one-size-fits-all rule.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Louis Ng touched on the role of NGOs and civil society.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These range from employment standards, supporting low-wage workers and retirement adequacy, to foreign worker management.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Going forward, I would like to assure Mr Ng Page: 121 that we will continue to engage our social partners as we try to shape the new employment landscape together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms ThanaletchimiI raised the issue of incentivising companies which hire older workers with lower foreign worker levies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, firms which hire older workers currently benefit from the Special Employment Credit.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This way, even firms without foreign workers can still benefit and be motivated to hire and retain our local older workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Lowering the foreign worker levy may also lead to the unintentional outcome of these companies hiring more foreign workers, instead of keeping our older workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having said so, if I may quote what Minister Tan Chuan-Jin said at last year's COS where this issue came up as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He said that the decisions on CPF top-ups and transfers between spouses are "personal decisions best left to the couples to decide.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It would be intrusive for the Government to intervene" by automatically optimising the split of CPF savings between husband and wife.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I must say that I do agree with him.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What I would do is that I would, together with CPF, step up the effort to create greater awareness in the community so that, hopefully, we get more and more members of the community to be fully aware of this additional interest that they can benefit from.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I hope that Members here can also help us to reach out to the ground.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chen Show Mao raised a question about Silver Support.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He asked whether it can be paid on a monthly basis, instead of a quarterly basis.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Minister for Finance has explained this in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Unlike Workfare, Workfare was given for work done earlier.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Workfare was paid after the work was done.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of Silver Support, we have decided to pay in advance.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we are paying quarterly payments in advance.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, in January, he will get the Silver Support for the next three months.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I appreciate Mr Chen's point that if it is paid out monthly, hopefully that will help to manage their finance better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But on balance, between giving them the money in advance to facilitate better liquidity versus giving it monthly to enforce them to spread the spending over three months, I think, on balance, the decision on advance payment quarterly would probably be more beneficial, given the flexibility.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I would say that we are very mindful of the sustainability of this scheme.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Right now, there is no plan to go for this adjustment according to inflation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, I think I have covered most of the cuts raised by Members.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I had in my cut earlier raised the plight of workers when companies are entering into liquidation, judicial management and various winding-up proceedings.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I hope MOM would partner the other Ministries to look into and review this area to see how best we can provide more safety nets for our workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, this question was raised by Mr Zainal Sapari to the Ministry of Law.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I do not have the date, but I think it was in January 2016.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: From our experience, a majority of local workers do indeed file their claims before this happens.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, when I was at NTUC, this was raised by the workers many times as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Each time we raised the retirement age or re-employment age, some workers would ask, "Why are you forcing me to work till an older age?" We explained to them that the purpose of retirement age, the purpose of re-employment age, is to protect the workers, give the workers the right to work.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, employers cannot simply "complete" the employment before the worker reaches the retirement age and now the re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, if we were to abolish the retirement age, the question is, "What will happen?" Are we giving workers more protection or less protection?

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank the hon Member for raising this very important question.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: As mentioned in my speech just now, we are focusing on a four-pronged approach to tackle, reduce and, hopefully, eliminate the workplace safety fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This is what we intend to do; that is, to raise awareness through a lot of media publicity and also public education programmes.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: Thirdly, to step up enforcement and lastly, to stiffen the penalties.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We discovered in the last few years that there are three areas that constituted the highest fatalities: fall from heights where workers work at heights, workplace traffic safety and crane safety.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: This year, we will be focusing on these three areas because they constitute the most numbers of the workplace fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We will work and step up and focus all our resources and Page: 123 manpower to deal with these three critical areas.

speaker: Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong
text: We also know that we need to go upstream to work with the companies and industries to introduce this idea called "Design for Safety" to make sure that when they start work or design something, they will always incorporate the ideas of workplace safety and health into the planning stage so that, upstream, they will be able to do something to prevent and reduce the downstream fatalities and accidents at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Mr Chairman, still on this subject of retirement age.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: I agree with Minister Lim that the statutory retirement age works towards protecting the workers, giving them the right and peace of mind and confidence to work.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: My clarification is on the other end of it.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: Although the statutory retirement age in Singapore now is 62, there are companies in Singapore today, for example, companies under the ComfortDelgro group which have done their own calculations and have implemented company policy to retire or offer retirement age above the statutory retirement age – that is, 65 or 67 – and there are other companies in Singapore doing the same.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: That also then fits the company's or the industry's own realities and it offers the employees added assurance as well.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How
text: So, my question to the Minister is whether the Ministry would consider that this is an area where the tripartite partners can work together on, to widen their awareness of this possibility, so that all companies can look at their situation and avail themselves and their workers of this option and possibility?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, I agree fully with Mr Heng Chee How.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When we prescribe laws and legislation, we are defining the minimum required standard.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, if any company were to behave in a way that goes below the stipulated requirement, then what they have done is illegal.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Companies would have to comply with the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Having said so, our objective is to encourage as many companies as possible to do better than what is prescribed in the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The example cited by Mr Heng Chee How is exactly what we call "progressive behaviours" which we would like to see more and more of in our industry.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In that regard, I fully agree with him that maybe TAFEP, as a tripartite alliance for fair and progressive practices can actually take on such a role to keep encouraging companies to do more, and MOM certainly will give our full support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: So, my question is: are we going too far in the opposite direction?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Assoc prof Randolph Tan for the two points.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will engage the companies and ask the companies to provide us with information of who are the workers, how many will be affected and, in terms of the job profile, how many are PMETs, how many are rank-and-file workers, and for each of these groups, what are the ages, background, and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And then, the other programmes will come in, like CSP, PCP and we will talk to the workers, introduce them to these schemes and bring them in.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The objective is to help them to go back to work as quickly as possible, both the PMETs and the rank-and-file workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Increasingly, the job matching is going to go beyond WDA and e2i.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Earlier, I mentioned that we intend to engage our Employment Agency industry more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because we believe that they, too, can have a role to play.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I would say that, on the whole, maybe we are doing too much compared to many other places.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But I must say that it is something which is very close to the hearts of the tripartite partners – NTUC, e2i and WDA.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We do feel very strongly that whatever we can do, we must help them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The weakness in our market today is we feel that the employment agency market is not job seeker-centric and so, their objective is really to help the companies find workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What we end up with is that the less employable workers are the ones who could end up taking a long time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: That is why we want to make sure that we do our best to support them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the question of action taken, again, employers, whether we are swinging too much, I am very mindful of that.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, earlier in my address, I emphasised very clearly that as Singapore moves forward, we must both become even more pro-business as we become more pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The two have to be the two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because if we are pro-business and not pro-worker, we can have a strong economy but weak Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Or if you are too pro-worker and not pro-business enough, we can have a strong Singaporean Core but a weak economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If there is a "triple weak", then there must be a "triple strong", and the two must go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For the "tripe weak", so far, we are starting with only the outliers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we look at sector by sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We look at each sector and we look at all the companies in the sector that employ EP workers and plot them in terms of their strength of their Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We can see a spread − industry norm somewhere in the centre, the "triple strong" on the extreme right, and the "triple weak" on the extreme left.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Hopefully, by sending Page: 125 this clear messaging, the rest will start to gravitate more towards the centre over time.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are very mindful that we have to strike a balance because, at the end of the day, if we swing too much to, as the Member said, against the employers, eventually we will be hurt.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because if Singapore loses its attractiveness as an investment location, eventually, we will run out of jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The best way to be pro-worker is to be pro-business because a job is the best welfare; full employment is the best protection.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we must always be mindful that Singapore is not just an economy; Singapore is a nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I always remember what our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew said.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He said that in nation-building, we must have three pillars, and this is what we call the Singapore software.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The first pillar is that our economy must always be competitive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because if our economy is not competitive, all of us will be poor together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, always be mindful that competitiveness in an economy is only a means to the end.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The end objective is social progress and social well-being, and employment is the best way for our people to benefit in its progress.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And lastly, he also mentioned the third pillar, and the most difficult pillar, is sustainable development.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: You can be pro-business today to ensure the economy is competitive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: You can be pro-people, pro-worker today, to ensure the society will be cohesive, we will have social progress.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But how do you strike a balance in such a way that we can sustain our development for the long term?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Every year, every three years and five years, when we adjust our Government policies, we are trying to define that balance.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, three years ago, there was no "triple weak" or "triple strong".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Today, we have "triple weak" and "triple strong".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Three years or five years from now, there could be something else, not because we have done something wrong in the past but rather because we keep striking that dynamic balance between the two.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I want to assure Assoc Prof Randolph Tan that I am very mindful of this and that I will always make sure that the interests of pro-business and pro-worker will always be harmonised and, hopefully, always strike the right balance.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am going to take one more last clarification.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, can you keep your clarification short?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have clarifications for the Minister concerning the response to workers who have been retrenched or made redundant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Government is saying that the main strategy will be, of course, to match jobs to skills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We hope all the three will come together quickly for people who are retrenched.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But, of course, that is always the case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It may take time for the correct match to happen.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: At the same time also, some of these workers who may lose their jobs may actually have other possible options which are better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Chairman, I agree fully with the first part but not the second part.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The first part, the Member talked about – for example, some of the retrenched workers who may have their own options in terms of becoming entrepreneurs and so on – that I fully agree.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, just recently, a business entity approached MOM and came up with this idea.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: His organisation – at this moment, I am not ready to disclose any information – is prepared to step forward to play a role.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because when a person becomes an entrepreneur, there are many things he needs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He may need advice on how to run a business, capital to start his business, and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, I would say that this is an idea worth exploring.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As I said, I fully agree with the Member's first part.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The second part is about insurance and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the future, hopefully, we can also include this entrepreneurship as one of the alternatives, something that I am very keen to work on.

speaker: The Chairman
text: That is about the time that we have for clarifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I believe this MOM COS debate has thrown greater light on the manpower challenges that we face as a country and the right things we must do to stay ready, relevant and resilient.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We know the workforce has to adapt and grow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Companies not just have to stay lean and productive but also have to be "triple strong".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: If I may quote Minister Lim Swee Say's famous proverb: "You need to be not just better but betterer and betterest" in terms of our tripartite relationship, labour management relationship and building a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: With that, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
